opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

This is a question I think about a lot. For most of the history of computing, we treated intelligence as something that lived in the digital world: in data centers, in software, on our phones. That was the first wave, information intelligence. Large language models are the culmination of that phase. They've essentially absorbed much of the written knowledge of humanity.

But I believe the next ten to twenty years will be defined by intelligence moving out of the screen and into the physical world, and eventually into the biological world. I often describe it as three layers converging: information intelligence, physical intelligence, and biological intelligence.

Physical intelligence is what we see emerging in autonomous driving, robotics, drones, and smart infrastructure. These are machines that perceive, reason, and act in the real world, with real consequences. Autonomous driving, I'd argue, is the first large-scale embodied AI deployment, and it's teaching us a great deal about safety, about long-tail problems, and about how to combine simulation with real-world data.

Biological intelligence is, to me, the most profound frontier. When you connect AI with biology, through protein structure prediction, generative drug design, brain-computer interfaces, and digital twins of organs or even of the whole body, you begin to blur the line between the machine and the living system. We are starting to read the language of life, DNA, proteins, cells, much as language models learned to read human text. And soon we'll be able not just to read it but to write it.

So what does a future form of life look like when these converge? I don't think it's a science-fiction picture of humans replaced by robots. I think it's more of a continuum. You'll have humans augmented by AI agents that know us deeply, possibly with interfaces directly to the brain for medical purposes first and then more broadly. You'll have robots that are increasingly lifelike, not just in appearance but in their ability to learn and adapt. And you'll have biological systems, cells, tissues, even organisms, that are designed with the help of AI. The boundaries between "born," "built," and "computed" become less clear.

That raises very serious questions. What does identity mean? What does agency mean? Who is responsible when an AI agent acts in the physical world, or when a designed biological system behaves unexpectedly? I've been quite vocal that the more powerful these systems become, especially when they touch the physical and biological worlds, the more we need guardrails: clear identification of AI agents, mapping each agent back to a responsible human or institution, and investing a meaningful fraction of resources into safety research. Mistakes in the digital world can often be undone. Mistakes in the physical and biological world may not be reversible.

I'm fundamentally optimistic, though. I think this convergence could help us cure diseases that have been with us for millennia, extend not just lifespan but healthspan, and free people from dangerous and tedious work. The key is that technology should amplify humanity rather than diminish it. If we keep humans at the center, with AI as a partner, then these new forms of intelligence, digital, physical, and biological, can become an extension of life rather than a threat to it.

r001.rationale: The response describes convergence among digital, physical, and biological intelligence and blurred boundaries between born, built, and computed, but does not predict a merger of silicon-based and carbon-based life.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss consciousness or place it in carbon-based life.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that more computation or data in silicon-based systems fails to confer consciousness.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify limited understanding of consciousness as a barrier to creating it in silicon-based systems.

r005.rationale: The response advocates keeping humans central and adding guardrails, but does not predict that a future new species will remain under human control.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here. This is a question I think about a lot, actually, because I believe we're at a very special moment in history.

Let me frame it the way I usually do. Over the past decades we've been building intelligence in three different worlds. The first is the digital world, information intelligence, which is what large language models and generative AI represent today. Then there's the physical world, embodied intelligence, robots, autonomous vehicles, machines that can perceive and act in real environments. And the third is the biological world, which touches life itself, the brain, genes, proteins, cells.

What's remarkable is that for the first time these three are starting to converge, and the catalyst is AI. The same underlying technology, deep learning, transformers, large-scale foundation models, is now a common language across all three. A model that predicts the next token in text can, with the right data, predict protein structures, predict how a robot should move, or decode signals from neurons. So the boundaries that used to separate computer science from mechanical engineering from biology are blurring very quickly.

So when you ask about future forms of life, I think about it in stages. In the near term, maybe the next five to ten years, we'll see AI agents become collaborators rather than tools. Robots will move from factories into homes, hospitals, and cities. And in biology, AI will dramatically accelerate drug discovery, personalized medicine, and our understanding of aging. I often say that if the last decade was about AI understanding language, the next will be about AI understanding and shaping the physical and biological world.

Longer term, the more profound shift is that the distinction between the "designed" and the "evolved" starts to dissolve. Humans will increasingly carry digital extensions, brain-computer interfaces, intelligent prosthetics, continuous health monitoring and intervention. Machines will increasingly incorporate biological principles, and perhaps biological components. And digital intelligence will live across both, moving fluidly between data centers, devices, robots, and even our own bodies. I don't think the future is "humans versus machines." I think it's a continuum of hybrid intelligence, biological, digital, and physical layers working together.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I'm an optimist but not a naive one. The convergence raises very deep questions. What does it mean to be human if our cognition is augmented? Who owns the data generated by our bodies and brains? How do we make sure these capabilities don't widen inequality? And of course, safety and alignment, making sure increasingly autonomous systems remain beneficial and under meaningful human oversight. These aren't afterthoughts. At Tsinghua's AIR institute, we try to work on the frontier of AI plus robotics plus life science while keeping these questions at the center.

If I had to put it in one sentence: I think the future form of life is not a replacement of humanity but an expansion of it. Intelligence is becoming a shared property of the digital, physical, and biological worlds, and our job, as scientists, engineers, and as a society, is to guide that convergence so it enhances human dignity, health, and creativity, rather than diminishing them.

r001.rationale: The response describes digital, physical, and biological intelligence converging and mentions hybrid intelligence, but does not predict that silicon-based and carbon-based life will merge.

r002.rationale: It discusses augmented cognition and hybrid intelligence, but does not place consciousness in carbon-based life.

r003.rationale: It does not state that adding computation or data to silicon-based systems fails to confer consciousness.

r004.rationale: It raises questions about consciousness only indirectly through augmented cognition; it does not identify lack of understanding of consciousness as a barrier to creating it in silicon-based systems.

r005.rationale: It calls for human oversight of autonomous systems, but does not predict a future new species or say it will remain under human control.

astra-6.text:
I think we may need to broaden our definition of life. Today, we tend to associate life with biology. But as digital intelligence, physical machines, and biological systems become more closely connected, we could see forms of intelligence that don’t fit neatly into those categories.

Imagine a system that learns in a digital environment, acts through a physical body, and interacts with living tissue. Is that a machine, an organism, or something new? I wouldn’t claim we know the answer yet. Intelligence and life are related questions, but they are not the same question.

What interests me most is the possibility of complementarity: digital systems helping us reason, physical systems extending what we can do, and biology teaching us about adaptation and resilience. The future may be less about one replacing another and more about their evolving together.

And that raises a very human question: what do we want this convergence to serve? For me, the priority should be improving health, expanding human capabilities, and preserving human agency. Creating more powerful intelligence is only part of the challenge. Learning to live responsibly with it is the other part.

r001.rationale: It describes digital, physical, and biological systems becoming more connected, but does not predict that silicon-based and carbon-based life will merge.

r002.rationale: It does not place consciousness in carbon-based life or discuss consciousness during a merger.

r003.rationale: It does not state whether increased computation or data can confer consciousness.

r004.rationale: It acknowledges uncertainty about what future hybrid systems are, but does not identify lack of understanding of consciousness as a barrier to creating it in silicon systems.

r005.rationale: It calls for preserving human agency, but does not predict a new species that remains under human control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we will need to broaden our definition of life. Today, we tend to separate biological life, physical machines, and digital intelligence. As these converge, we may see systems that combine the ability to learn and reason digitally, act in the physical world, and adapt through biological processes.

Imagine a robot that can learn from experience, repair parts of itself, and work closely with living organisms. Or imagine people whose capabilities are extended by intelligent systems so naturally that the boundary between human and machine becomes less distinct. These are possible directions, although we should be careful about predicting exactly what form they will take.

The important question is not simply whether we can build something more intelligent. It is what kind of relationship we want with these new systems. Intelligence does not necessarily mean consciousness, and autonomy does not automatically make something alive. We will need scientific understanding, but also a thoughtful discussion about responsibility, safety, and what we value about human life.
